The text is badly corrupt throughout, especially the opening period (the clauses on what Easter does are syntactically broken; 'bonus tumet' and 'subit odium' are rendered tentatively) and the fractional reckonings. Roman fraction terms (as = unit, here a whole day; uncia = 1/12; quadrans = 1/4; dodrans = 3/4; deunx = 11/12; sicilicus = 1/48; scripulum = 1/288; decussis = 10, tressis = 3) are rendered by sense; 'sela', 'circunsela/cincunsela', 'trion', 'habeo' are unclear and kept as they stand. The Agriustia passage ('semispuncla, duoque habeo. Devidentur foris exclusæ') is largely unintelligible. 'Agriustia' is probably a corruption of the name of the computist Agriustia/Agrestius; 'Thimidensium regiorum' taken as Thimida Regia in Africa. 'Augustalis' is the author of an earlier 84-year Easter table. 'Ocdoada/endecada' = ogdoad/hendecad (8- and 11-year segments of the 19-year cycle). 'Non lavorabis' read as 'non laborabis'. 'Fabulis' near the end read as 'tabulis'/'fibulis' (tables). The Zechariah quotations follow the text's corrupt Old Latin wording.

The arithmetic in ref 2 is badly transmitted. 'nungenti triginla milia sex unus' is taken as 931 (84 × 11 1/12), which the following total (30,667) requires. The quotient '25,908' should probably be 25,980 (779,402 ÷ 30). 'sextus vicies quinque' is obscure and perhaps stands for 'eighty-four times twenty-five'. 'bismilies' and 'septaes, quattus super et septus' are corrupt; [...] marks words that cannot be construed. 767,025 ÷ 7 is exactly 109,575. 'decus quattus' is taken as fourteen (decies quater). The fractions follow the earlier rendering (bes = two-thirds, sicilicus, selae of a scruple). 'recalato tempore' is unclear. 'regis Geiserici decimo anno' refers to the Vandal king Geiseric. 'per Moysen ... in mense novorum' renders the Old Latin 'month of new things'. In the Exodus quotation, 'in mensibus fasae' seems corrupt for 'in mensibus anni' and is translated so. Elsewhere in ref 3, 'filiorum Dei' is taken as '[as Son] of God', and 'vi facere' as 'et facere'.

The text of both passages is badly corrupted, and many of its numbers do not add up. Line 4: 'luna vigesima, et secunda feria septima' is taken as 'the twenty-second moon, the seventh weekday'. 'luna VII' is probably meant for 17. 'Agriustia' is an unidentified name and is probably corrupt. 'semipsum' (here and in line 5) is read as 'assem ipsum', 'that same day'. The fraction calculations attributed to Agriustia are garbled and have been rendered as far as they can be followed. 'selae' is an unexplained fraction term, possibly a corruption of 'sextulae' or 'sicilici'. 'docies' presumably stands for 'octogies' (384). The sum of the two hendecad and second-cycle totals is given in the text as 6,666, but it must be 30,666. Line 5: 'venter et te( tum' is unintelligible and is marked [...]. The arithmetic gives 779,031 where the text has 779,301, and 779,402 where the text has 709,400; the text's figures are translated as printed. The sentence beginning 'Submit your hard necks' and the sentence on the moon's creation ('ut de noctis invenies lumen solidatae tenebrari ob nubimenta tenuaret... cautis vacasse per erroribus') are corrupt, and their translations are conjectural. 'ad alhomum' is unintelligible. 'decus dipondius' is taken as twelve and 'decus tresis' as thirteen.

The stretch is a single long reference, so it is rendered as one line. Several corrupt places are translated by their evident sense. 'ut ritis cornibus extenuatur' is read as 'attritis cornibus extenuata'. In 'supputatio pronuntiat luna' a word seems lost after 'luna', marked [...]. 'Lunaris autem annus aeque in sex mensibus dividitur' is translated with '[pairs of]', since the arithmetic (6×29 + 6×30) requires twelve months. 'centus octo' is read as 180 (centum octoginta), as the total 354 requires. 'sexes vies nonus' is read as sexies viceni noveni (6×29). 'cc. decusas' is read as 210. 'Osius' is read as Josias (Josiah); in Latin Bibles this book is often 3 Esdras / 1 Esdras. 'existis' is read as 'ex istis'. In the final sentence, 'refallatur' is read as 'refellatur'. The dates of the moon's months do not all match a strict 29/30 alternation; they are translated as printed.

nodes.text: THE ANONYMOUS LITTLE BOOK ON THE CALCULATION OF EASTER.

While an inquiring mind was toiling with special eagerness over so weighty and so very desirable a matter, and had persisted long in reading, panting [for an answer], namely [concerning] that [feast] which cleanses a man entangled in mortal snares and purified from his offences by fasts, and joins him to the choir of the blessed, which shows the garment of baptism, spattered with scarlet stains and another's red, as white as snow on the candidate, which also receives into the wedding of the Lamb [one] swollen with long-standing sins, which raises up one fallen in the collapse of ruin, [making him] by the prayers of the priests a restored temple for the Lord, and [where] hatred enters, it has shone with the brightness of compassion, a light of knowledge shone forth, so that those things which seemed to one searching and longing to be darkened by certain clouds might be laid open, and all hidden things might be uncovered to him, by whom the courses of the moon might be firmly established in full, and the Easter cycles, agreeing with one another and with the lunar years and the headings of the embolisms, might be known without any error by the ignorant; in these the years of the ogdoads and hendecads are so investigated, and, completed by divine will, so marked, that they seem not to waver in any way at all. On them, it is recognised, so great a marking has been fixed by the providence of the Creator that in the tenth year of King Geiseric four hundred and twenty years from the Lord's Passion were completed at the head of the first ogdoad, and such an Easter, both of the Jews and of the Christians, was found as was then celebrated by the Lord with his disciples. He suffered for us on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the sixteenth moon, the sixth weekday, and rose from the dead on the sixth day before the same Kalends, on the eighteenth moon, the first weekday, as in the first year of the first ogdoad of the work undertaken is shown beyond doubt to our eyes by truthful evidence. For the present year in the first ogdoad is the four hundred and twenty-sixth from the Lord's Passion, in the sixteenth year of the King; and the head of the second cycle has its year in the consulship of Theodosius for the seventeenth time and of Festus, at the end of which two thousand one hundred years were completed from the sons of Israel going out of Egypt, and an Easter was found such as had first been sacrificed by the Fathers in Egypt; and in the sixteenth year of the King two thousand one hundred and sixteen are noted, in the twenty-sixth cycle, the seventeenth year of the same cycle, in which year the Lord's Easter is kept on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, on the seventeenth moon. But that one as [i.e. one whole day] more is found in this cycle, and it turns back again from the second moon to the head, the lunar fractions produced this, because within twelve years, so that we might announce the Easter days in full, one as will clearly be found from the accruing twelfths, besides, that is, that as of the weekdays which over four years is very often added for the leap day. Therefore eighty-four times [an as and] a twelfth [make] seven and seven tens [and] two [asses]: you have eighty-four years, in which Augustalis, of most holy memory, noted six of the seven asses in his ogdoads and hendecads not in their proper places and seats; these the annual twelfths produced over eighty-four years. For this reason error is sometimes found in his cycles, while the number of years and the courses of the elements are not attended to clearly enough, although one as of seven is always deducted in eighty-four years, and is never at all admitted to the Easter calculation; and that same as, being inattentive, he did not insert in its proper place in the lunar course—or rather he set it aside as superfluous to complete demonstrations. It is this which is recognised as begetting the Easter errors, as is shown by the series of years written out. But so that you can find that as which is excluded, you will have to use [perhaps this] calculation. For eighty-four times ten [and] a twelfth make you nine hundred and thirty-one days; divide by thirty, you will find thirty-one [and] a remainder: these are the thirty-one embolisms which every table is known to have; there remains that one as which at the end of eighty-four years is always deducted from the seven, and which, as we have said, the lunar fractions produced as superfluous. This also Agriustia, of that municipality of Thimida Regia, writing to Hilarianus on the Easter reckoning, wished to exclude by a certain art through scruples, relying for each year not on eleven days and twelfths, but on eleven days [and] half-twelfths, two selae, his scruple, a quarter-twelfth, two selae, less by two scruples [and a] circunsela to a twelfth, which make in eighty-four years two hundred and four scruples [and a] sixth, which are eight hours, a half-point, and two habeo. They are divided, excluded outside. So, to make up a full day to be excluded from the number seven, three hours, eleven scruples, ten points are lacking; therefore he was certainly unable to determine some years fully by his demonstrations. Foreseeing, then, that this as must by all means be set aside, [I say] that if Augustalis had, as I said, inserted the six asses in fixed numbers in the members of the table, he would by no means have fallen into fault in the lunar course and the Easter years; from which outcome of error he is seen to have put this as forward superfluously and variously in his lunar course; and by a smaller element the lunar course is concluded in the third cycle, in the twenty-fourth year of thirty. It also agrees with these Easter cycles over eighty-four years, and when these are completed you return to the head, whether in the lunar lattices or in the Easter years. Of these, then, the seventeenth year [falls] in the sixteenth year of the King; but in the lunar course, as we have said, within twelve years you insert one as into the first, second and third lattice, above what the Kalends of January had; thus too you are supported by truth for each year. So when in the third lattice you have reached the twenty-fourth year, you will return after eighty-four years, having excluded one day from the number seven, coming from the lunar increments, and you will find at the head of the lattices the second moon; in these ten letters are counted from A to K, which [sic] set out their own days, so that the monthly number is carried on. These, then, are known to be fixed outside through the twelve months, from which letters you look out the era for each day; and so, descending straight down in the lattices year by year, having followed the line against that era, you will be able to find most truly which moon it is, being indeed taught by the knowledge of the heart. In the lattices of the weekdays an indication is given to the searcher by the number seven; for from A to G seven letters are noted, in which the seventh year is kept, where for the leap day you insert one as every three [times] four years, that is one year K., and whatever [day] you wish to look up in the order of the months, [taking] the era you see noted at the head for each day, against it in the same lattices you will find the fixed weekday. In the leap-year column, which, glued to the lunar lattices, is joined by a fixed boundary. The seventeenth year itself, then, [is] the third weekday; but where you find the day of the Kalends of March marked in red, there you have the leap day marked by an inserted weekday. When you have reached the twenty-eighth, you will return to the first year; and so, recapitulating to the end of the world, you will find noted each of the years, Easter as well as leap years, and at the same time also the lunar years and the days of the week. But so that you may recognise the leap day itself fully, you will have to follow this reasoning and know that you will not work on this leap day. The Hebrews first, for this reason, taught not by their own wisdom but by God's, could not err about the course of the moon; and therefore, when they first sacrificed the passover in Egypt on the day before the Ides of April, the fourth weekday, the fourteenth moon, two-thirds [and a] sicilicus, two selae of a scruple, three, a half-twelfth, a sicilicus, they said 'twelve of the waning and twelve of the waxing'; because they found that the moon, when it was made, began from diminution, not from increase; from which it is understood that the equinox, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, was found to be the first day, and that on the fourth day, which is the fifth before the same Kalends, almighty God said: 'Let there be two lights in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth, and divide between day and night, and let them be for signs, and for times, and for days and for years, and let them be in splendour in the firmament of heaven so that they may shine upon the earth; and so it was done. And God made two great lights: the greater light the beginning of the day, and the lesser light the beginning of the night'; and so on. Almighty God therefore made the sun the beginning of the day, and it ran eleven hours and a quarter of an hour before the moon was made; and at once he commanded the moon to be made and to follow it, with which she had obtained so great an office in heaven. She was established, therefore, full, on the fifteenth, because the power of the Creator produced nothing that was not full and perfect. And therefore indeed it was said, 'twelve of the waning and twelve of the waxing'; for the moon wanes through twelve half-months and waxes through twelve half-months, so that what the sun is known to have run short of a full day, this the moon is found by the wise to have diminished [by] divine instruction; and so when the Lord commanded [her] to wax by three-quarters and wane by three-quarters, as the calculated division shows, whether in the thing or before it. For fifteen times three-quarters [make] ten [and a] quarter; but because he said 'twelve of the waning and twelve of the waxing', a twelfth part of ten [and a] quarter will make you eleven-twelfths [and a] sicilicus. The lunar year has three hundred and fifty-four days, in a month of which year you will find twenty-nine days [and a] half, to which you will add eleven-twelfths [and a] sicilicus, and you get thirty days, five-twelfths [and a] sicilicus. So twelve times thirty [and] five-twelfths [and a] sicilicus make you, according to the Roman reckoning, three hundred and sixty-five days [and a] quarter; this quarter you will bring together over a period of four years, and it makes you one as, the leap day, that is four quarters of an as; this is one weekday. Concerning the columns which are drawn with their lines at the head of the cycles, this reasoning is shown, emblazoned, to whoever desires it. For whatever the moon was on the Kalends of January, having followed the line straight against it, you will find. In the second column, on what day of the first month [falls] the first moon, fixed before your eyes; in the third, fourth, fifth and sixth column, on what [day] the tenth moon will be of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth month—seeing this line with your eye, you observe it arranged through four columns. For it is noted as serving the lawful fasts, as the most holy Moses testifies of the fast of the seventh month at the Lord's command: 'Thus says the Lord: from the ninth of the month,' he says, 'to the tenth of the month at evening you shall keep your sabbaths; and everyone who has not humbled himself in that fast, I will destroy that soul from its people.' So also through Zechariah, the glory of all the Prophets, the Lord spoke after the time of the captivities concerning these sacred lawful fasts, saying: 'The word of the Lord almighty came to me,' he says, 'saying: Say to the people of the land and to the priests: If you have fasted and lamented in the fifth or seventh fasts, and behold, for seventy years, did you fast a fast for me, O house of Israel? And if you eat and drink, do you not eat and do you not drink [for yourselves]? Are these not the words which the Lord spoke by the hands of those prophets who were before us, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, and its cities round about, and the hill country and the plains were inhabited?' And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying: 'Thus says the Lord Almighty: Judge just judgement; show compassion and mercy each to his brother; and do not oppress the widow and the orphan and the stranger and the poor; and let none of you keep the malice of his brother in your hearts.' And a little later: 'Thus says the Lord Almighty: the fourth fast, and the fifth fast, the seventh fast and the tenth fast shall be for the house of Judah for joy and for gladness and for good festivals; and you shall be glad, and you shall love truth and peace.' See how the lawful fasts ought to be kept is announced by the Lord. But why they are assigned to these months, let us show to those who wish [to know]. For the fourth fast [is] for first-fruits and the months; and we fast the fifth fast for gathering in the threshing-floors and offering tithes; the seventh fast for gathering the vintage; and the tenth fast for the sowings, also of seed, and for offering the first-fruits of oil. In the four weeks of these fasts you will see the tenth moon, manifest, without any error. From the Lord's Easter of each year you count eighty-four days, at the end of which you will find the sabbath day, which is the end of the week that contains the tenth moon of the fourth month, and you will discharge the fourth fast after the sacrifice. One hundred and twelve [days] the fifth fast; one hundred and seventy-five the seventh fast; two hundred and sixty-six the tenth fast; thus, reviewing each in order, the master and teacher of this art will be able to find them, provided that drowsiness of heart, which the wise avoid, does not overwhelm the understanding. To these columns mentioned above seven others are joined, in which the moon of the Kalends of January and the Sundays of Easter are noted; for the thirtyfold number of the moon, divided by the sevenfold number of the week, marks off two hundred and ten spaces. And to find the day of each Easter, you will observe the moon and the weekday that fell on the Kalends of January, so that, keeping to the moon's course in the same column, you may find the day of Easter which appears to belong to the weekday written above; the same is confirmed also in the thirty tables that follow, in which you will find noted the moon and weekday of the Kalends of March, by the number seven of each in a moon of thirty days, [making] two hundred and ten spaces, announcing most certainly the fixed Sunday Easter of each year. For three other columns follow the number of these tables like attendants, which are made to show more plainly to the curious and the very careful, by stretched lines from the Kalends of January, the headings of the embolisms and the lunar years, what [moon] it was, so that the truth of these cycles may be displayed adorned in all its jewels.
BOOK TWO, WHICH CONTAINS ALL THE ADORNMENTS OF THE CYCLES.

We have also, with the Lord's assent, shown another reckoning plain, concerning the twenty-fifth cycle, that it contains two thousand one hundred years, namely from the most holy day of the passover sacrificed in Egypt, so that you may observe that on the Kalends of January the second moon, and the fourteenth [moon] of the first month on the day before the Ides of April, and the fourth weekday were fixed entire at the head of the second cycle; and you, a most diligent searcher, reckoning it, must find it in this way. For eighty-four times three hundred and fifty-four make for you twenty-nine thousand seven hundred and thirty-six lunar days; and eighty-four times eleven and a twelfth make for you nine hundred and thirty-one embolismic days; add [these] to the sum above, and you have thirty thousand six hundred and sixty-seven days. From this subtract one day, which we teach in what follows to have been produced from the lunar losses, and we show most plainly how it is removed. Therefore one cycle has eighty-four years, which contain thirty thousand six hundred and sixty-five nights. And since the twenty-fifth cycle from that same passover was completed in the consulship of Theodosius for the sixteenth time and Faustus, reckoning it with the time recalled, you will find that it has seven hundred and sixty-six thousand six hundred and twenty-five nights; when you divide these into a sixtieth part, you will find twelve thousand seven hundred and seventy-seven [and] a twelfth; when you add this sum to the sum above, it makes seven hundred and seventy-nine thousand four hundred and two nights; dividing these by thirty you will have twenty-five thousand nine hundred and eight, with a dupondius [and] a twelfth over; this, I say, was the second moon on the Kalends of January. Behold, thanks be to God, how worthily and rationally the second moon was found on the Kalends of January, which, producing the fourteenth of the first month together with the heading of the embolism, is found in every case. So from these very Kalends of January, so that you can find the fourteenth [moon] on the day before the Ides, reckoning up to the third day before the Ides of April, you have one hundred and one days; to these days add the second moon, which was found on the Kalends of January themselves, and they make for you one hundred and three days; divide by sixty, you have two-thirds [and a] sicilicus, two selae of a scruple, a third, twelfths, a sicilicus; add this to the one hundred and three days, and they make for you one hundred and four days, two-thirds [and a] sicilicus, two selae of a scruple, a third, a half-twelfth, a sicilicus; divide by thirty, you will find three, and fourteen over, two-thirds [and a] sicilicus, two selae of a scruple, a third, a half-twelfth, a sicilicus; and you have the fourteenth [moon] of the first month, and what runs over, on the day before the Ides of April, which is the first most holy day of the passover. But so that you may find the fourth weekday of this fourteenth moon, [the day] of the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, pay attention: for the twenty-fifth cycle is found to have been concluded at the end of the second table [counting] from the children of Israel going out of Egypt, as the sixth [...] twenty-five times of the years indicates through the history of the law. If, then, eighty-four [times twenty-five] make two thousand one hundred passovers, and at the head of the twenty-sixth cycle two thousand one hundred years are completed, [...]; accordingly [two thousand] one hundred times three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter make for you seven hundred and sixty-seven thousand and twenty-five days. Divide these by seven and you have one hundred and nine thousand five hundred and seventy[-five], [...] over. Begin to count from the first weekday, which fell on the Kalends of January themselves in the first year of the passover sacrificed in Egypt, from the first unit to seven units, and you will find the seventh weekday on the day before the Kalends of January, and the first weekday on the Kalends of January themselves; from the day of these Kalends reckon to the day before the Ides of April, and you will find one hundred and two days. Divide these by seven, and you have fourteen, with four over; this is the fourth weekday of the fourteenth moon of the first month of the first year, as we said, at the head of the second cycle, in which we found the most holy passover sacrificed then by the fathers in Egypt. But when you have attentively followed these cycles in order, you will find the true days of Easter noted within the columns, and [you will see] that those which are outside, written most falsely and carelessly above the brow of the columns, were without doubt fixed in error. You see, then, dearest ones, that Almighty God denies nothing to any one of us: but whatever anyone has presumed of him, does he not bestow it lavishly, as he wills, on one who desires faithfully? For he commanded these mysteries to be made manifest in such a way that in the four hundred and twentieth year from the Lord's passion, in the tenth year of King Geiseric, we should find the day on which the Lord ate the most holy passover with his disciples; and that in that same [year] two thousand one hundred and ten years should be completed, namely from that yearling lamb without blemish sacrificed in Egypt, as they are shown headed in order from the head of the second cycle.

Let us begin, then, brothers, by recalling to the memory of those who know, from the reading of Exodus, that lamb sacrificed in Egypt, so that we may show to those who wish the appearance of both lambs. In that reading we recognise that our God and Lord himself said to Moses and Aaron his brother in the land of Egypt: 'This month,' he says, 'shall be for you the beginning of months, the first among the months of the year,' saying to the whole congregation of the children of Israel: 'On the tenth day of this month let each take for himself, by the houses of the tribes, a sheep for each house; and if they are too few in the house to suffice for a sheep, let them take with them their nearest neighbour; according to the number of souls, each according to what will suffice them, they shall reckon for the sheep. The sheep shall be without blemish, unspotted, perfect, male and a yearling it shall be for you; you shall take it from the lambs and from the kids, and it shall be kept by you until the fourteenth day of this month. And all the multitude of the congregation of the children of Israel shall kill it at evening; and they shall take of its blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel in the houses in which they eat it, and in them they shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire, and they shall eat it with unleavened bread. You shall not eat it raw, nor boiled in water, but roasted with fire: the head with the feet and the inner parts, leaving nothing of them until morning, and you shall not break a bone of it. Whatever is left of it until morning shall be burnt with fire. And you shall eat it thus: your loins girded, and shoes on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste, for it is the passover of the Lord.' So Almighty God commanded through Moses the whole congregation of the children of Israel, in the month of new things, which is the beginning of months among the months of the year, in what dress they should eat the passover; for this purpose, surely, that he might both manifest his divinity to us who believe in Christ, and show their banditry already then, from the first passover celebrated in Egypt; for they, in Egypt at evening, that is, in the last times of the world, girded and shod, went out at evening on the first day of unleavened bread with swords and clubs against the unspotted Lamb of God, and committed against him everything that had been foretold of him by all the Prophets. And therefore we, who now celebrate the passover not according to the image, as they did, but according to the truth, in commemoration of the passion of the Son of God, ought first of all to inquire diligently, with all the strength of our faith, into nothing else than the coming of our Lord himself, and then turn back to the series of the cycles. For first Gaius Julius Caesar ruled at Rome for ten years, four months, six days. After Gaius Julius Caesar the emperor Augustus succeeded, who ruled at Rome fifty-six years, four months, one day. In his reign came John, son of Zechariah the priest, sent by God, preaching the baptism of repentance, who, in accordance with the preaching of the law and of all the prophets, showed Christ, [showed] that Christ the Son of God had come into this world, that is, into the region of Judaea, saying: 'This is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world; and this is the Saviour of the world; this is he of whom I said: A man has been made before me, the strap of whose shoes I am not worthy to loose.' From then Jesus began to teach the people and to do mighty works and great signs, which no one else had done. And after his baptism he manifested himself to the whole human race as [Son] of God, sent by God the Father to establish, reform and reconcile to himself the people he had formed. Having chosen twelve disciples, power was given to them in the Holy Spirit; and he sent them through all nations, so that being taught they might teach. Then, having appointed them to the office of preaching the grace of God brought about through his name, the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, eternal life for the dead who rise again, he foretold to them how much he would suffer from the Jews, even to death, the death of the cross, and that he would remain three days in the heart of the earth, and that on the third day he would rise from the dead, and after the resurrection would go to heaven. Then Tiberius Caesar ruled twenty-two years, seven months, twenty-two days. In his reign, that is, in the sixteenth year of his rule, when Pontius Pilate was procurator of Judaea, under the priests Annas and Caiaphas, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the two Gemini, there fell the sixteenth moon, the day of preparation, when our Lord, the Saviour of the human race, Jesus Christ the Son of God, suffered. Having endured, then, all that had been written of him, according to the preaching of the law and of all the Prophets and of his Gospels, he suffered, as we said, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the day of preparation. And on the third day he rose from the dead, on the Lord's day, the sixth day before the same Kalends, and having spent about forty days with the Apostles and Disciples, he was received into heaven, wrapped in a cloud. From then, therefore, with the grace of God reigning, people believing in his name began to be enlightened. And therefore in all these things let us give thanks to him who arranges all these things for our salvation; and the Lord God Almighty, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, calls us to divine knowledge; to him be honour and glory through the same Lord Christ in the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

So from the first-formed Adam to the sixteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, that is, to the day of the Lord's passion, there are 5,500 years, and from the Lord's passion to the tenth year of the King, 420 years; in that year you will also find the most holy day of Easter on which our Lord was sacrificed for us as the lamb of God. This day is fixed at the head of the first cycle in the tenth year of the same King, headed with a complete number. In these years, then, Augustalis, the author of his own table, although he was endowed with knowledge of letters and skilled in the art of calculation, is known to have fallen into error. The cause was the number of years in his lunar course, to which one whole day too many is proved to have accrued from that deceptive number of years. For he says that in the 186th year from the Lord's passion, on the same day of Easter, day matched day, whereas he ought to have found that day in the 169th year from the head of the third cycle; he is known to have fixed it in his cycles in the 69th year. But that day without members, dressed up with a name, he is shown to have headed among us in the seventeenth year, at the head of the arrangement of his cycles, in an uncertain number; and so he certainly seems to have fallen into error, as he himself admits in his address. 'But as for the fact that the cycles of years have not been arranged from the year in which the Lord suffered,' he says, '[this is] the usefulness of the compendium as worked out and found: from the two Gemini consuls, in whose year the Lord suffered, to the year of the consulship of Antoninus for the fourth time and Albinus, which is the first in this work, 186 years are counted; and since it happened in this same consulship that the day of Easter agreed in every way with the day of the Lord's passion, the usefulness of the completed (sic) compendium ought not to have been scorned.' From this consul, then, in whose year the beginnings of the first ogdoad were made, up to the year in which the eighty-fourth year is closed with its signs of embolisms, it is very easy for those who look to prove the truth of the cosmic calculation with their own eyes as witnesses, just as he promises to prove himself in this reckoning. Yet he neither fixed the day of the Lord's passion wholly at the head of his first ogdoad, nor truly determined the certain number of years. This is shown by the text of our following cycles. At their head you find, on the Kalends of January, the twenty-second moon, the seventh weekday; the fourteenth [moon] of the first month on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, the fourth weekday; and Easter Sunday on the sixth day before the Ides of April, the eighteenth moon. At the head of his cycles, by contrast, there is on the Kalends of January the 20th moon, the 6th weekday; the fourteenth of the first month on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the 5th weekday; and Easter Sunday on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the 7th moon. On this day he thinks the Lord's passion fell, which in no way agrees with the truth. So too the little lunar course itself, radiant with its ruddy light, shows it to our sight, and with it the number of years rightly fixed in its sure place. But Agriustia, first cultivator of perversity, lover of his own error and most unskilled teacher of his own assertion, tries to scatter that same day, which we said must be removed, by scruples across the single years. So let his falsity be shown plainly and laid bare, and let him be seen to be a stranger to the truth. Let him now be pressed with more learned questions: by what argument of consolation, as it were, did he choose to extend the moon's increase in the course of the year in his tables as eleven days, a half-twelfth, two *selae*, one scruple, a half-twelfth, two *selae*, and not as eleven days and a twelfth? Beyond doubt the same moon testifies that it increases by this amount in the annual separation itself. Through this twelfth, in 84 years, the reckoner could have had seven days. Of these, it was fitting (sic) that he should have removed one day, which runs after thirty-one in the time of Moses, and recognised the full truth. Eighty-four times, then, as he says, a half-twelfth, two *selae*, one scruple, a half-twelfth, two *selae*: he himself answered, 'six days, a quarter, eleven scruples, five-sixths' (sic); that is what he asserts. And he says the six are six days, and the quarter is three hours, but the eleven scruples and five-sixths (sic) are proved to be two points short, since ten points are most clearly recognised to be contained in a five-sixths. What could be plainer in this question, what more probable in his answer, than that the inept man should be defeated by his own kindling? Having let slip whole eight hours, he strove by his suspicions and practice to exclude only two points, at the will of his own judgement, and was quite unable to remove the full day. For this reason he has taught all heretics (sic) to fall away from the rule of truth, so that, like men already made blind, they could no longer find the door of light. But let it be shown how, with sure numbers, [the day] is removed for the prudent, and a sense that has grasped [it] whole will not delay to turn [it] aside. For eighty-four times 354 are 29,736 days; and again eighty-four times eleven days and a twelfth make you 931 days. Added to the sum above, these will be 30,667 days. These days are known to be so determined by ogdoads and hendecads that they excluded the superfluous day they contain and recorded a certain number enclosed within themselves. For there are five ogdoads and four hendecads. The five ogdoads there have fifteen embolismic and twenty-five lunar years, and 495 months, which contain 14,614 days. The hendecads there, embolismic and lunar, have twenty-eight [years] and 544 months, which yield 16,056 days. When you add the sum of these days, they make you 30,666 days. See: from 30,667 days one day is briefly excluded in the ogdoads and hendecads, truly proved by the division of days, and yet it is scattered by the unskilled and the eager in their disputes. So too in the following cycle, in twin concord with the one above, through the embolisms and common years, you, curious one (sic), will very quickly find that same day fully removed. For in the second cycle, as in the first, there are 31 embolismic years and 53 common ones. Thirty-one times 384, then, gives you 11,904, and fifty-three times 354 make you 18,762 days. These two small sums joined together make 30,666 days, and that aforesaid day is removed.

Let us return, then, to that sum in what was said above concerning that year [...], by which you learned that in the first year of the passover celebrated in Egypt the second moon fell on the Kalends of January. If you are willing to attend to it, you will remove this same day most fully. For the aforesaid sum contains 766,625 days. From these deduct 365 days, namely those of the last year of the cycles, so that it may appear that this day too, born of the septenary number from the increase of twelfths, was excluded through this sum. Learn also that the twenty-first moon of the eighty-fourth year is fully bare, without twelfths. And when you restore the aforesaid days to the sum above and divide it, you will find the second moon, which you know was marked on the Kalends of January at the head of the second cycle by the hand of the one who spoke. With these 365 days deducted, then, 766,260 days remain. Divide these by sixty and you will have 12,771; add this to the aforesaid sum, and there will be 779,301 days. Divide these by thirty and you will find 25,967, with 21 days over. These are the twenty-first moon of the eighty-fourth year. When the aforesaid 365 days are restored to that sum above, there will be 766,625 days, as above. Divide these by sixty and you will find 12,777, a twelfth; add this to the aforesaid sum, and you have 709,400 days, a dupondius, a twelfth. Divide these by thirty and you will have 25,980, with a dupondius and a twelfth over, just as the moon is headed at the head of the second cycle; and you will be brought to that same day which we have very often said must be removed at the end of the cycles. Whoever you are, then, wounded by the guile of madness or ignorant of this reckoning, recognise through what high and deep sum of division (or rather, to speak more truly, through what clear demonstration) this day was excluded from the septenary number. If you have been unable to remove a whole [day] in your reckoning, you are found a novice on both counts. Stop, I beg, stop now pressing wretched peoples into error through deceit with your little subversions. Submit your hard necks at last to the truth, you who, through mists and illusions, [come as] a messenger of the most holy day of Easter, as though it came to you from Egypt, from unknown stretches of provinces and long distances of lands, to be celebrated out of season and very often in vain. For when you glue the lunar course of these cycles into the sense of your heart, then you will find a true foundation from the first year of the passover sacrificed in Egypt, which you know to be quite consistent with both the true lunar lattices and the Easter headings. You already know from what was said above that the second moon was found and held at the head of the cycles on the Kalends of January. From those Kalends you will reckon to the day before the same Kalends of January of the following year, and there will be 365 days. To these add the second moon, which fell on those same Kalends, as he said [...], and they make 367 days. Divide these by sixty and you will find six days, a twelfth, two *selae*; add this to the aforesaid sum, and you have 373 days, a twelfth, two *selae*. Divide these by thirty and you will find twelve; there is over thirteen, a twelfth, two *selae*. You must reckon in the same way in the following year, which is called third in order. Twice 365 make 730 days. Put in, as above, the second moon of the first year, and you will have 732 days. Divide these by sixty and you will find twelve; two *selae* remain. Add this to the aforesaid sum and there will be 744 days; two *selae* remain. Divide these by thirty and you will find twenty-four days, with twenty-four over; two *selae* remain. In this way you will reckon each single year up to the eighty-third year; the eighty-fourth you recognise as noted at the end of the cycles. So you will be seen to put in eleven days and a twelfth in each of these years, and you will be known not to have erred at all in the windings of the lattices or in the lunar headings. For our Lord Christ, obeying his Father's command, so brought forth the kindly star of this moon that [...] it might thin the clouds of the darkness of night [...]. Borne on a clear course, free from errors [...], with secret causes at work, it now withdraws when full, to be filled again, and with its revolving courses is bounded once more. These, then, are the beginnings of the moon and its duties, divinely established in perpetual service; these were made foreknowing in signs and in seasons and in days and in years. Through this chaste and pure fabric, and as a foreshadowing of his majesty, the Lord signified with respect to the church that it is very often thinned by various misfortunes and is always diminished in the lapsed, yet, supported by the brightness of its splendour, it grows in the saints. To say it specifically: the church itself speaks thus of itself: 'I am dark,' it says, 'and comely, O daughters of Jerusalem.' And the Lord answered that ringing voice through the Prophet, saying: 'You are all beautiful as the sun, and perfect as the moon.' And again: 'Once I have sworn by my holy one: I will not lie to David; his seed shall remain for ever, and his throne as the sun in my sight, and as the moon perfect for ever.' This whole mystery remains for the church in Christ and belongs to it. For we most attentively represent the most perfect course of the same moon, so that you may know it to be wholly bounded, in a way, within its lattices on each single day. From the Kalends of January, I say, you will reckon to the day before the day on which you are seeking the moon's age. But perhaps you say: why [reckon] to the day before and indicate the moon's age on the following day? Because you gather the sum from the Kalends of January and put in on top the age the moon had on them. Could you in any way count one day, split in two or doubled, as a single one in the number? So divide these by sixty, and put the result of your division above the number of days. Divide these likewise by thirty, and on any day, as I said, you will most skilfully mark what age the moon will be, [...] through each single day and year. It is true that the birthday of every Easter is generated only by the new day of the first month. But that this first month is commonly said by all to run from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April, let it be shown by sure and ordered reasoning, so that the birth of Easter may be uncovered within these twenty-nine days and shown more clearly through the first annual cycle by true proofs. For from the making of the sun and moon, which took its beginning on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, we reckon that 340 free days ran to the coming fifth day before the Nones of March. To these days we add the fifteenth moon, the fullness in which the moon had been set by the Lord at evening on that same fifth day before the Kalends of April, and they make 355 days. Divide these by sixty, and you have five, eleven-twelfths; Add [this] to the sum above, and they make 360 days and eleven-twelfths. Divide by thirty and you will find twelve, with one and eleven-twelfths over. And since the fifteenth moon, full, as we said, had been made on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, on the day before the Ides of April, its horns worn away and thinned, it completed its first month. For this reason the Jews were commanded to observe the new moon down to the present day. It completed the second month on the fourth day before the Ides of May, the third month on the fourth day before the Ides of June, the fourth month on the sixth day before the Ides of July, the fifth month on the sixth day before the Ides of August, the sixth month on the seventh day before the Ides of September, the seventh month on the day before the Nones of October, the eighth month on the Nones of November, the ninth month on the day before the Nones of December, the tenth month on the third day before the Nones of January, the eleventh month on the Kalends of February, the twelfth month on the fifth day before the Nones of March. And you have 355 days, which the first year contains, there indeed with fifteen days of the moon, at which age it had certainly been made full and complete. For from the fifth day before the Nones to the fourth day before the Nones of March the reckoning declares the moon [...], that is, the day midway between the fifth and the third, on which the moon was found to be eleven-twelfths and not a whole unit, which is one full day. Therefore the first month cannot begin from that day, but from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April. On the day before that fourth day before the Nones, that is, on the day of the Kalends of April, we reckon from the fifth day before those same Kalends of the past year, that is, the first year, on which day both lights had been set by the Lord for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years; and we shall find 370 days. To these we add the fifteenth moon, the state in which it had meanwhile been made, and they make 385 days. Divide these days by sixty, and you have six and five-twelfths. Add these to the aforesaid sum, and they make 391 days and five-twelfths. Divide by thirty and you will find thirteen, with one and five-twelfths over. Therefore we must look for the first moon from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April, since on whichever of these twenty-nine days the first moon falls, from there the first month begins, in which month almighty God commanded the most holy Easter to be celebrated, as he testifies in Exodus, saying: 'You shall keep the feast day of the Passover; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time of the month of new things; for in it you came out of the land of Egypt.' Again in Leviticus the Lord commands, saying: 'In the first month, on the fourteenth of the month, in the midst of the evenings, is the Passover of the Lord, and on the fifteenth of this month the feast day of unleavened bread to the Lord.' Again in Numbers: 'And the Lord spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai, in the second year after they set out from Egypt, in the first month, saying: Tell the children of Israel to make the Passover at its time, on the fourteenth day of the first month at evening. According to its times, according to its law and according to its ordering you shall do it. And Moses told the children of Israel to make the Passover in the desert of Sinai; according as the Lord commanded Moses, so the children of Israel did.' And a little after, the Lord commanded with a threat, saying: 'The man who is clean, and was not on a long journey, and has failed to make the Passover, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he did not offer a gift to the Lord at its time; and that man shall bear his sin.' In Deuteronomy Moses spoke to the people, saying: 'Observe the month of new things, and make the Passover to the Lord your God, because in the month of new things you came out of the land of Egypt by night; and you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God.' So too in the first book of Ezra it is written more plainly: 'Josiah kept the Passover to God in Jerusalem, and sacrificed the *phase* on the fourteenth moon of the first month at evening.' See: the day of the fourteenth moon, which runs from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, is recognised as established lawfully and by true reasoning. And so also from the third day before the Nones of March to the tenth day before the Kalends of April there are nineteen days, in which, when the moon is born, it is without doubt assigned to lunar years; but from the ninth day before the Kalends of April to the fourth day before the Nones of the same there are ten days, and when it is born in these it is certainly noted as fixed to embolismic years, as is proved in the index of the cycles of antiquity. For six months divide the year, but in the embolismic one a month of thirty days is added as an extension. Six times twenty-nine, then, make you 174 days, and seven times thirty you have 210; join the small sums, they make you 384 days. This is the embolismic year. The lunar year is likewise divided into six [pairs of] months. So six times twenty-nine make you 174 days, and six times thirty are 180. The small sums joined together make 354 days, reckoned not from Easter Sunday to Easter Sunday, but from the fourteenth to the fourteenth moon of the first month of the coming year. And so you will find all the days gathered in their order through eighty-four years in fixed months without doubt, just as the appearance of the moon's own birth shines out month by month, with the eyes as witnesses. For from the first moon on the Kalends of January up to the eighth you will find embolismic years; from the ninth to the twenty-seventh you will surely find lunar ones. So also from the twenty-eighth to the thirtieth you will find embolismic years. You will observe all these things carefully, and you will find the day of Easter entire. You will not toil: see, with the Lord's assent, each thing is shown clearly and completely, by which the bad faith of detractors is now refuted, so that the shrewd simplicity of the innocent may be known, made subject to all, and the errors of hypocrites avoided; for boasting belongs to the unskilled, whereas the virtues mentioned above are full of modesty.
